newsitem.title: FRANCE: Agnelli sees Europe at risk if EMU delayed -paper.
newsitem.headline: Agnelli sees Europe at risk if EMU delayed -paper.

text.p: Italian tycoon Giovanni Agnelli said in a newspaper interview to be published on Friday that if European monetary union (EMU) was postponed, it risked not happening at all and Europe would suffer as a consequence.

Agnelli told the French newspaper Le Figaro that EMU should group as many countries as possible at the outset. If Italy is not deemed ready to join in the first wave in 1999, an accord should be signed to schedule its entry soon afterwards, he said.
An advance copy of the interview was sent to Reuters.
Agnelli also said Britain would have no choice in the end but to join EMU.

He said the real problem facing Europe was whether it would become a competitive region or go into decline. "The only way to make Europe competitive is to create a unified economy. A single currency is just one step," he said.
"It's important to make the effort now...All the experts agree -- if we don't create a single currency on the scheduled date, we risk putting it off forever," he said.
"...I think everyone should join, even if they're not altogether ready in a convincing way," he said.

"...In the event -- and I hope that's not the case -- that Italy is not in a position to join from January 1999, an accord must be signed so that (Italy) can join later, a year later for instance. That wouldn't be a tragedy," he said.

He said Italy had made enormous efforts since 1992 to improve its finances and attain the standards set by the Maastricht treaty on the establishment of a single currency. Agnelli said Italians had paid 420,000 billion lira ($247 billion) in supplementary taxes since 1992 as part of this effort.
"Our government has bet everything on Italy joining from 1999," he said. If Italy did not take part at the outset, he said, elections might have to be called.
He said he understood the concerns expressed in some quarters in Germany about the southern European countries' taking part in monetary union.

"I can see very well that the (German) central bank would have concerns. It's already been through a very difficult situation with East Germany. That could be repeated with southern Italy or other under-developed regions in the Mediterranean," he said.

But Agnelli said he believed the Germans were wary rather afraid of including southern Europe. "When the Germans think of a Europe without the Mediterranean, they very quickly become sad. It's true. Europe without the Mediterranean and its culture would be a very sombre thing," he said. "It's also true they see it as a factor of trouble."
Agnelli said that although the British have not made up their minds, "I have the impression they won't have any choice."

"Britain's foreign policy has always rested on three pillars -- the Commonwealth, Europe and the United States. The Commonwealth's influence has been reduced greatly. The United States is closer to Europe as a whole today than to Britain. Finally, can you imagine for an instant The City outside the single currency?"
